newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: German envoy pledges help in Colombian kidnap case.
newsitem.headline: German envoy pledges help in Colombian kidnap case.

text.p: Germany's ambassador to Bogota has pledged to help clarify the case of a shadowy German private eye arrested on kidnap charges, Colombia's Foreign Ministry said on Sunday.

In a meeting with Foreign Relations Minister Maria Emma Mejia on Saturday, the newly appointed envoy, Geert Hinrich Ahrens, also apologised for remarks made recently in the German Bundestag by Bernd Schmidbauer, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's head of intelligence services.

The talks appear to have taken place in an effort to head off a growing political and diplomatic scandal sparked by the arrest of Werner Mauss on Nov. 17 as he tried to smuggle German Brigitte Schoene, who had been kidnapped by Colombian rebels, out of the country.
"Ahrens presented a report on behalf of the German government about the facts surrounding the case of (Werner Mauss, who was) recently arrested in Colombia," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

The Colombian authorities said Mauss was an international head of the National Liberation Army (ELN), the country's second-largest guerrilla force. They were apparently unaware of Mauss' negotiations to free Schoene.
Bonn has maintained, meanwhile, that it was "fully informed" of Mauss' operation, which it described as a "humanitarian" rescue mission.

Schmidbauer, who was Mauss' direct contact in the German government, raised Bogota's hackles when he told German lawmakers earlier this month that Mauss' undercover mission was indispensable, since leftist rebels controlled half of Colombia.

"That was a total misunderstanding. Anybody who follows the Colombian situation knows that the government has not ceded sovereignty of any part of the national territory," Ahrens told Mejia, according to the official statement.
The German envoy, who took up his post at the outbreak of the Mauss scandal, said Bonn fully "respects the principle of nonintervention in Colombia's internal affairs."
Mauss and his wife are both in custody in the northwest city of Medellin, facing charges of aggravated kidnapping and conspiracy to abduct.

In a communique published over the weekend, ELN leaders denied Mauss was linked to the rebel army and said neither they nor Mauss had played a role in kidnapping Schoene but had merely mediated her release.
Schoene, the wife of a former BASF Chemicals executive based in Colombia, returned to her home near Medellin after she was freed on Nov. 17.
